svg.aria-label: Diagram: what consumes the AWS STS session token budget and what changed. On the left, the inputs that spend the budget when a session is created: session tags, of which up to 50 may be passed with a tag key limit of 128 characters and a tag value limit of 256 characters; session policies, where the passed JSON policy document and all passed managed policy ARN characters combined cannot exceed 2,048 characters, with a maximum of 10 managed policy ARNs and only one JSON document; and identity provider attributes carried through federation. A note records that AWS recommends passing session policies through the CLI or API because the Management Console might increase the session token size by adding session information. In the centre, the change: previously there were separate limits on session token size and on passed-in parameters, and now STS enforces a single 4,096-byte limit on the session token. On the right, what is new for operators: response elements report session token size and percentage utilisation relative to the limit, those values are logged in CloudTrail and published to CloudWatch, and an optional API parameter generates deliberately larger tokens up to the limit so applications and infrastructure can be tested against the bad case. A panel at the bottom records the deprecation that the announcement omits but the IAM quota reference states: the PackedPolicySize response element is deprecated and AWS directs customers to use SessionTokenUtilization instead, so any tooling reading the old element is reading a deprecated field that measured something different.
svg.title: One budget, several spenders, and finally a way to read it
svg.text: A limit you could hit, but never measure
An oversized session token fails in a proxy or a gateway — never in the component that grew it.

fails — before it does in production.
The deprecation the announcement does not mention
From the IAM quota reference: “The PackedPolicySize response element is deprecated. Use SessionTokenUtilization instead.”
They do not measure the same thing. One was the packed size of the policies you passed — a component of the problem.
The other is the percentage of the token limit consumed, which is what decides whether the call works at all.
Grep for PackedPolicySize. It is a definite audit with a definite answer, and it is the one action this release actually requires.
Then read the utilisation figure for your worst real session — the one with the most tags and the largest policy. That number is your headroom.
